pos: a. (ravenous, insatiable; in the Authorized Version chiefly greedy of gain and greedy of filthy lucre, a disqualification for office)
etymology: Old English graedig, hungry or covetous. The Hebrew idiom at Proverbs 1:19 is botsea batsa, one who cuts off gain by violence; the Greek at 1 Timothy 3:3 is aischrokerdes, eager for shameful profit.
biblical_def: Scripture almost never uses greedy of the stomach; it uses it of gain. “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Proverbs 1:19) — the Hebrew pictures a man cutting off a profit by violence, and the proverb notes that the profit destroys the one who takes it. The household consequence is stated plainly: “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27). Isaiah turns the word on shepherds, which is to say on ministers: “Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain” (Isaiah 56:11). Paul takes it up as a formal disqualification for church office in both lists — an overseer must be “not greedy of filthy lucre” (1 Timothy 3:3), and so must a deacon (1 Timothy 3:8). The Greek aischrokerdes names not the amount but the appetite: money loved for itself, sought in ways that shame the seeker. The word describes a settled orientation of the heart, which is why it bars a man from office rather than merely calling for his correction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines greedy as having a keen appetite, ravenous, and figuratively as eager to obtain, especially of money.
webster_full: GREEDY, a. Having a keen appetite for food or drink; ravenous; voracious; very hungry.
2. Having a keen desire for any thing; eager to obtain; as greedy of gain.
They are greedy dogs which can never have enough.
GREEDINESS, n. Keenness of appetite for food or drink; ravenousness; voracity.
2. Ardent desire; as greediness of gain.
scriptures: Proverbs 1:19
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
Proverbs 15:27
He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.
Isaiah 56:11
Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter.
1 Timothy 3:8
Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;
corruption_summary: Greed has been reclassified as ambition and rebranded a virtue, while the specific disqualification of a greedy minister is quietly ignored.
corruption_paragraphs: In the commercial register greed has been laundered into drive, hunger, or ambition, and it is now praised in the same terms Isaiah uses to condemn: a man who can never have enough. Scripture does not object to profit, to industry, or to wealth honestly gotten; Abraham, Job, and Boaz were all rich men. It objects to the appetite that makes gain the end, and it says twice what that appetite costs — it takes away the life of the owner, and it troubles his own house. Proverbs 15:27 sets the antidote in the second clause: he that hateth gifts shall live. The bribe refused is the mark of the man not ruled by gain.

The graver corruption is inside the church, and Isaiah aimed at it first. Greedy dogs are shepherds; the men who cannot have enough are ministers. Paul made freedom from that appetite a condition of holding office — not an area for growth, a condition — and the modern church has largely stopped applying it. Where a ministry is structured so that the preacher's income rises with the intensity of his appeals, 1 Timothy 3:3 has been suspended in practice however loudly it is affirmed on paper. The apostolic remedy was structural: Paul would not handle the collection alone, and he worked with his own hands rather than be chargeable to any.
roots_summary: Hebrew botsea batsa, one greedy of unjust gain — Proverbs 1:19, 15:27; az nephesh, strong of appetite — Isaiah 56:11; Greek aischrokerdes, eager for base gain — 1 Timothy 3:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew batsa — to cut off, to gain by violence; the noun is unjust profit, Proverbs 1:19.
Hebrew az nephesh — strong of soul or appetite; Isaiah 56:11, of shepherds who can never have enough.
Greek aischrokerdes — greedy of shameful gain; 1 Timothy 3:8 and Titus 1:7, both office qualifications.
Greek pleonexia — the desire to have more; Colossians 3:5, where it is named idolatry.
Old English graedig — hungry, covetous; the root of the English word.
usage: “Greedy of gain” — the Authorized Version's standing phrase, and it takes the owner's life.
“Greedy dogs which can never have enough” — Isaiah's verdict on hireling shepherds.
“Not greedy of filthy lucre” — a bar to office, not a matter for improvement.

pos: n. (one who eats to excess; in the law, a capital charge against a rebellious son, and in the Gospels a slander against the Son of man)
etymology: From Latin gluto, a glutton, from glutire, to swallow, through Old French gluton. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 21:20 is zolel, a squanderer or riotous eater; the Greek slander at Matthew 11:19 is phagos, an eater.
biblical_def: Gluttony appears in the law not as a private failing but as evidence in a capital case. The parents of the stubborn son bring their charge to the elders: “This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard” (Deuteronomy 21:20). The two vices are named together because both are the visible fruit of a will that has thrown off authority; the sin prosecuted is the rebellion, and the appetite is the proof of it. Proverbs keeps the pairing and adds the outcome: “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Proverbs 23:21), following the warning not to sit among “riotous eaters of flesh” (Proverbs 23:20). Then the word is turned into a slander against our Lord. “The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). John came neither eating nor drinking and was called demon-possessed; Christ came eating and drinking and was called a glutton. The generation was not evaluating conduct at all — it was refusing both messengers — and our Lord's answer is that wisdom is justified of her children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a glutton as one who indulges to excess in eating, and figuratively one greedy of anything to excess.
webster_full: GLUTTON, n. One who indulges to excess in eating.
2. One eager of any thing to excess.
GLUTTONY, n. Excess in eating; extravagant indulgence of the appetite for food.
Their sumptuous gluttonies and gorgeous feasts.
APPETITE, n. The desire of food or drink; a painful sensation occasioned by hunger or thirst.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 21:20
And they shall say unto the elders of his city, This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard.
Proverbs 23:21
For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
Proverbs 23:20
Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
Matthew 11:19
The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.
corruption_summary: Gluttony is the one deadly sin the modern church has stopped naming, having outsourced the whole subject to dietetics and body image.
corruption_paragraphs: Of the traditional catalogue of grave sins, gluttony is the one now almost never preached. Two pressures produced the silence. The first is that the subject has been transferred wholesale to medicine and diet culture, where the categories are health, metabolism, and appearance rather than sin, appetite, and self-government — so a pastor who raises it sounds as though he is commenting on his people's bodies. The second is that gluttony is the respectable indulgence of respectable congregations, and men do not readily preach against what they are doing. Scripture keeps it in the list, pairs it with drunkenness every time, and treats both as marks of a will that will not be governed.

The correction must run in both directions. Naming gluttony is not licence to make the body itself the measure of holiness; that is its own ancient error, and the apostle warns against a will-worship of neglecting the body that has no honour in satisfying the flesh. The biblical category is appetite ungoverned, which can be as true of a thin man as a heavy one. Deuteronomy 21:20 is the key: the charge is rebellion, and the eating is evidence. And Matthew 11:19 stands as a permanent guard against the opposite excess, since our Lord Himself — who fasted forty days and also came eating and drinking — was called a glutton by men who simply would not receive Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew zolel, a riotous eater or squanderer — Deuteronomy 21:20, Proverbs 23:21; Greek phagos, an eater — Matthew 11:19; Latin glutire, to swallow.
roots_lines: Hebrew zolel — one who is vile, a squanderer, a riotous eater; Deuteronomy 21:20 and Proverbs 23:21.
Hebrew soba — drunkard, the constant companion term in both texts.
Greek phagos — an eater, a glutton; Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:34, both in the mouths of accusers.
Greek gaster — the belly; Titus 1:12, “slow bellies,” and Philippians 3:19, “whose God is their belly.”
Latin gluto, from glutire, to swallow — the source of the English word.
usage: “He is a glutton, and a drunkard” — the appetites cited as evidence of rebellion.
“Drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” — the poverty that follows the table.
“Behold a man gluttonous” — a slander against Christ, and the proof they would receive no messenger.

pos: n. and v. (dissolute excess, wasteful revelry; the manner in which the prodigal spent his portion, and a bar to the eldership if found in a man's children)
etymology: From Old French riote, a dispute or debauch. The Greek at Titus 1:6 is asotia, literally unsavedness — the condition of one past saving from his own excess; at 2 Peter 2:13 it is truphe, soft living.
biblical_def: The Greek word behind riot at Titus 1:6 and Ephesians 5:18 is asotia, formed from the negative and the root of sozo, to save — an unsaveable wastefulness, the ruin a man works upon himself. It is the adverb of the same family that describes the prodigal, who “wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luke 15:13). Paul makes it a matter of church order: an elder's children must not be “accused of riot or unruly” (Titus 1:6), for a man's household is the visible test of his rule. Peter observes that the world finds abstention offensive: “Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you” (1 Peter 4:4). The believer who withdraws is not merely different; he is resented, and the resentment turns to slander. Peter's harshest use lands on false teachers who “count it pleasure to riot in the day time” (2 Peter 2:13) — the daylight detail is deliberate, for even the world's debauchery ordinarily hides itself, and these had lost the shame that covers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines riot first as wanton and unrestrained revelry or excess, and then as a tumultuous disturbance by an unlawful assembly.
webster_full: RIOT, n. In a general sense, tumult; uproar; hence technically, a tumultuous or violent disorder of three persons or more.
2. Uproar; wild and noisy festivity.
3. Excessive and expensive feasting; luxury.
RIOTOUS, a. Luxurious; wanton or licentious in living.
2. Consisting of riot; tumultuous; partaking of the nature of an unlawful assembly.
scriptures: Titus 1:6
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.
Luke 15:13
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
1 Peter 4:4
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
2 Peter 2:13

And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;
corruption_summary: Riot is now described as a lifestyle stage a young man passes through, and Titus 1:6 is treated as an unreasonable standard rather than a plain one.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has narrowed riot to a street disturbance and lost the older and more searching sense of wasteful, dissolute living. That narrowing is convenient. When the word means only a mob, no respectable man is guilty of it; when it means asotia — the self-ruining excess of the prodigal — a great deal of ordinary Western life comes under the term. The years of a young man's dissipation are now described as a phase, a season of finding himself, or simply as youth; Luke 15 describes them as wasting a father's substance in a far country, and the parable does not soften it before the young man comes to himself.

In church order the effect has been direct. Titus 1:6 makes the conduct of an elder's children evidence in the assessment of the man, and the requirement is regularly set aside as harsh or as unfairly holding a father responsible for adult choices. The text does not say a man's children must be sinless; it says they must not be accused of riot or unruly — not notorious for dissolution, not ungovernable. That is a public, observable standard, and it exists because the same qualities that govern a house are the qualities that govern a congregation. Where the standard is quietly dropped, the office is not made kinder; it is made hollow.
roots_summary: Greek asotia, unsaveable excess — Titus 1:6, Ephesians 5:18; asotos as adverb — Luke 15:13; truphe, soft living — 2 Peter 2:13.
roots_lines: Greek asotia — from a-, not, and sozo, to save; wastefulness past recovery. Titus 1:6, Ephesians 5:18, 1 Peter 4:4.
Greek asotos — the adverb, “riotously”; Luke 15:13, of the prodigal's spending.
Greek truphe — luxury, soft living; 2 Peter 2:13, of daylight indulgence.
Greek komos — revelling, a carousal; Romans 13:13 and Galatians 5:21, in the works of the flesh.
Old French riote — a quarrel or debauch; the source of the English word in both its senses.
usage: Asotia: literally unsavedness — excess that ruins the one who practises it.
“Wasted his substance with riotous living” — the prodigal's account in a phrase.
“They think it strange that ye run not with them” — abstention resented, then slandered.

pos: n. (the wringing of money from another by force, threat, or the abuse of a position; named in the temple, in the prophets, and in the apostolic list of those to be put out)
etymology: From Latin extorquere, to twist out, from ex, out, and torquere, to twist — the same root as torture. The Hebrew at Ezekiel 22:12 is osheq, oppression; the Greek at Matthew 23:25 is harpage, plunder or seizure.
biblical_def: Extortion is theft carried out under colour of right, and Scripture is unsparing with it. Ezekiel puts it in the indictment of Jerusalem: “In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 22:12). The closing clause is the diagnosis — the forgetting of God is what makes the wringing of a neighbour possible. Our Lord applies the same word to the religious leadership: “ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Matthew 23:25). The Greek harpage is the violence of a bird of prey, and the woe is not that the Pharisees kept the outside clean but that the vessel they polished had been filled by plunder. The Pharisee in the temple thanks God he is not an extortioner (Luke 18:11) — and goes down to his house unjustified, which is the sharpest possible comment on self-assessment in this matter. Paul lists the extortioner among those with whom the church is not to eat (1 Corinthians 5:11), placing him beside the fornicator and the idolater as a subject of discipline.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extortion as the taking of money by force or oppression, especially by an officer of justice under colour of his office.
webster_full: EXTORTION, n. The act of extorting; the act or practice of wresting any thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power.
2. In law, any oppression by color or pretense of right; particularly the taking of money by an officer, by color of his office, either where none is due, or more than is due.
3. Force or illegal compulsion by which any thing is taken from a person.
EXTORT, v.t. To draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, violence, authority, or by any illegal means.
EXTORTIONER, n. One who practices extortion.
scriptures: Ezekiel 22:12
In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD.
Matthew 23:25
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
Luke 18:11
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
1 Corinthians 5:11

But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
corruption_summary: Extortion is imagined as a crime of the alley, and Scripture aims it at respectable men using lawful position to wring their neighbours.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular picture of extortion is a threat delivered in a dark street. Webster's legal definition is closer to the biblical use: any oppression by color or pretense of right, and particularly the taking of money by an officer under colour of his office. Ezekiel is not describing gangsters but the princes, priests, and prophets of Jerusalem. Our Lord is not describing thieves but the men who tithed mint and anise. Extortion in Scripture is what men in authority do with the leverage their authority gives them, which is why it can coexist with a scrupulously clean exterior — and why the cup was full.

1 Corinthians 5:11 keeps the word from becoming an abstraction. The extortioner is listed among those a church must not sit down to eat with, and the list concerns men called brethren. This is the discipline the New Testament actually prescribes for a professing believer who wrings his neighbour, and it is almost never applied — partly because the sin is hard to see when it wears a contract, and partly because the men most able to commit it are often the men a congregation can least afford to lose. Luke 18:11 stands over the whole subject as a warning: the man most confident he is no extortioner went home unjustified.
roots_summary: Hebrew osheq, oppression or extortion — Ezekiel 22:12; Greek harpage, plunder — Matthew 23:25; harpax, a robber or extortioner — 1 Corinthians 5:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew osheq — oppression, extortion, gain wrung from another; Ezekiel 22:12 and Leviticus 6:4.
Greek harpage — the act of seizing, plunder; Matthew 23:25 and Luke 11:39, of the inside of the cup.
Greek harpax — ravenous, an extortioner; 1 Corinthians 5:11 and 6:10, and of wolves in Matthew 7:15.
Greek pleonektes — a covetous man, one who has more at another's cost; the companion term in Paul's lists.
Latin extorquere, to twist out — the root also of torture; the violence is in the word.
usage: “Gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me” — the two clauses belong together.
“Within they are full of extortion and excess” — a clean cup filled by plunder.
“I am not as other men are, extortioners” — and he went down to his house unjustified.

pos: a. and n. (irrational, of the beasts; used by Peter and Jude of false teachers who reason no higher than instinct)
etymology: From Latin brutus, heavy, dull, irrational, through French brut. The Greek at 2 Peter 2:12 is alogos, literally without reason or without word — the negative of logos.
biblical_def: Peter and Jude both reach for the same image when they describe false teachers, and the Greek word is exact: alogos, without logos, without reason or word. “But these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not; and shall utterly perish in their own corruption” (2 Peter 2:12). Jude states the same in a different order: “these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves” (Jude 10). The charge is not that these men are unintelligent — false teachers are frequently clever — but that in the realm where reason matters most they operate by instinct alone. They rail at what they cannot understand and understand only what an animal understands. The Psalmist had already drawn the line: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish” (Psalm 49:20). Honour without understanding is beast-life with a title. Agur uses the cognate against himself in a very different spirit — “Surely I am more brutish than any man” (Proverbs 30:2) — and that confession is the beginning of the wisdom the false teachers never reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brute as senseless, irrational, and as a noun a beast, any animal destitute of reason.
webster_full: BRUTE, a. Senseless; unconscious; as the brute earth.
2. Irrational; ferine; as a brute beast.
3. Bestial; in common with beasts; as brute violence.
BRUTE, n. A beast; any animal destitute of reason, and of course the word includes all animals except man.
BRUTISH, a. Insensible; stupid; unfeeling; savage; ferocious; gross; carnal; bestial.
scriptures: 2 Peter 2:12
But these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not; and shall utterly perish in their own corruption;
Jude 1:10
But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.
Psalm 49:20
Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.
Proverbs 30:2
Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man.
corruption_summary: Modern anthropology erases the line between man and beast, and then wonders why men behave as Peter said they would.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's image depends on a boundary: man is not a brute, and a man who lives as one has fallen below himself. Contemporary anthropology denies the boundary at the root, describing man as a more elaborate animal whose reason, conscience, and moral sense are behaviours selected for their advantage. If that account were true, Peter's insult would be a compliment and Jude's charge would be a description of everyone. Genesis 1:27 draws the line the apostles assume: man alone is made in the image of God, addressed by God, and answerable to God. It is precisely because he is not a brute that behaving as one is a ruin rather than a return.

The second observation is pastoral and cuts against pride. The men Peter calls brute beasts were teachers with a following, and Jude says they knew some things naturally — they were competent in the realm of appetite and advantage. Cleverness is no protection; a man may be sophisticated in everything except the one thing needful. Agur's confession is the antidote and the contrast: I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. The one who says that of himself is on the road to wisdom; the one Peter describes never says it at all.
roots_summary: Greek alogos, without reason — 2 Peter 2:12, Jude 10; Hebrew baar, brutish — Psalm 49:20, Proverbs 30:2; Latin brutus, dull.
roots_lines: Greek alogos — without logos, irrational, speechless; 2 Peter 2:12 and Jude 10, of false teachers.
Greek phusikos — natural, by mere instinct; joined to alogos in 2 Peter 2:12.
Hebrew baar — to be brutish or stupid; Psalm 49:20 and Psalm 73:22, “so foolish was I, and ignorant.”
Hebrew behemah — a beast, cattle; the animal to which the senseless man is compared.
Latin brutus — heavy, dull, irrational; whence English brute and brutish.
usage: Alogos: without reason — the charge is not stupidity but instinct where reason is owed.
“Man that is in honour, and understandeth not” — rank without understanding is beast-life titled.
“I am more brutish than any man” — Agur's confession, and the road to wisdom.

pos: a. (unfaithful after the manner of a harlot; used by the prophets chiefly of Israel's heart toward the LORD, and by Proverbs of a woman who hunts a man's life)
etymology: From Old English hore, a prostitute, with the adjectival -ish. The Hebrew at Ezekiel 6:9 is zanah, to commit fornication — the standard prophetic verb for covenant infidelity, applied to the nation far more often than to any individual.
biblical_def: The prophets use this vocabulary as covenant language before they use it as moral language. “I am broken with their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and with their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols” (Ezekiel 6:9) — the LORD speaks as a husband, and idolatry is adultery because the covenant at Sinai was a marriage. Ezekiel presses it further: “How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman” (Ezekiel 16:30), where the shocking detail is that Judah did not even take payment — she hired her lovers, which no harlot does. Hosea says the same of the mechanism: “the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God” (Hosea 4:12). Proverbs applies the adjective to an actual seductress and states the price: “For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life” (Proverbs 6:26). Both uses reinforce one doctrine — unfaithfulness is not a lesser sin of the appetites but a betrayal of a covenant, and it ruins the one who commits it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines whorish as lewd, unchaste, incontinent — the plain word for an unfaithful character.
webster_full: WHORISH, a. Lewd; unchaste; incontinent; addicted to unlawful pleasures.
WHOREDOM, n. Lewdness; fornication; practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex.
2. In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God, for the worship of idols.
ADULTERY, n. Violation of the marriage bed.
2. In a scriptural sense, all manner of lewdness or unchastity, as in the seventh commandment.
scriptures: Ezekiel 6:9

And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, because I am broken with their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and with their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations.
Ezekiel 16:30
How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman;
Proverbs 6:26
For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.
Hosea 4:12
My people ask counsel at their stocks, and their staff declareth unto them: for the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God.
corruption_summary: The prophetic marriage metaphor is dismissed as ancient misogyny, and with it goes the doctrine that idolatry is personal betrayal of a divine Husband.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern objection to Ezekiel 16 and Hosea is that the imagery degrades women, and the chapters are consequently skipped, apologised for, or read as evidence of an outgrown patriarchal outlook. The objection misreads the figure at its centre. The whorish woman in these prophecies is not a female character being shamed; she is Israel, a nation of men and women, and the men who first heard Hosea were told that they were the unfaithful wife. The metaphor humbles the male hearer by putting him in that position. Nor is the divine Husband coldly punitive: I am broken with their whorish heart. That is the language of grief, not contempt, and Hosea was commanded to buy his wife back.

Removing the metaphor costs a doctrine. If idolatry is merely an intellectual mistake about metaphysics, then repentance is merely correction; if it is adultery against a Husband who bound Himself in covenant, then repentance is the returning of a spouse and the mercy that receives her is astonishing. Proverbs 6:26 keeps the plain-sense application alongside, and does so without flattery to the man: the adulteress hunts the precious life, and the fool who is hunted is the one being warned. The New Testament keeps both senses — the church is the bride of Christ, and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery.
roots_summary: Hebrew zanah, to commit fornication, used of covenant infidelity — Ezekiel 6:9, Hosea 4:12; zonah, a harlot — Proverbs 6:26; zenunim, whoredoms — Hosea 4:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanah — to commit fornication; the prophets' standard verb for Israel's idolatry, Ezekiel 6:9.
Hebrew zonah — a harlot; the participle used substantively, as at Proverbs 6:26.
Hebrew zenunim — whoredoms; Hosea 4:12, “the spirit of whoredoms.”
Hebrew naaph — to commit adultery; the companion verb, and the seventh commandment.
The covenant at Sinai is described as a marriage, which is why idolatry is prosecuted as adultery.
usage: “I am broken with their whorish heart” — the LORD grieves as a husband, not merely as a judge.
“The work of an imperious whorish woman” — Judah hired her lovers, which no harlot does.
“The adulteress will hunt for the precious life” — the price stated in Proverbs.

pos: adv. (luxuriously, in self-indulgent softness; twice in Revelation of Babylon and the kings who lived so with her)
etymology: From Latin deliciae, delight or luxury, from delicere, to allure. The Greek at Revelation 18:7 is streniao, to live in wanton luxury — a word suggesting strength spent on self, related to strenos, the insolence of plenty.
biblical_def: Twice in the dirge over Babylon the Authorized Version uses this adverb, and both times it stands beside pride. “How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her: for she saith in her heart, I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow” (Revelation 18:7). The measure of the judgment is set by the measure of the luxury, and the boast that runs with it is a boast of invulnerability — I shall see no sorrow. The kings share the sentence: “the kings of the earth, who have committed fornication and lived deliciously with her, shall bewail her” (Revelation 18:9). The Greek streniao is stronger than the English suggests; it is not enjoyment but wanton excess, luxury with insolence in it. James uses the parallel charge against the rich who oppress: “Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter” (James 5:5) — the fattened beast unaware of the appointed day. Our Lord tells the same in the rich man “clothed in purple and fine linen” who “fared sumptuously every day” (Luke 16:19), with Lazarus at the gate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deliciously as in a delicious manner, delightfully, and notes the scriptural sense of luxurious living.
webster_full: DELICIOUSLY, adv. In a delicious manner; delightfully; as, to feed deliciously; to be deliciously entertained.
DELICIOUS, a. Highly pleasing to the taste; most sweet or grateful to the senses; affording exquisite pleasure.
2. Most pleasing to the mind; yielding exquisite delight.
DELICACY, n. Fineness of texture; softness; smoothness; elegance.
LUXURY, n. A free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table; voluptuousness in the gratification of appetite.
scriptures: Revelation 18:7
How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her: for she saith in her heart, I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow.
Revelation 18:9
And the kings of the earth, who have committed fornication and lived deliciously with her, shall bewail her, and lament for her, when they shall see the smoke of her burning,
James 5:5
Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter.
Luke 16:19
There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:
corruption_summary: Luxury is now treated as self-care and its purchase as a moral achievement, while Revelation 18 attaches judgment to the boast that goes with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Advertising has taught two generations to describe indulgence as something owed — a deserved reward, an act of caring for oneself, a treat one has earned. The vocabulary is therapeutic and the effect is to place luxury beyond moral examination altogether, since to question it is to be unkind. Revelation 18:7 makes the examination anyway, and it does so by quoting the heart: I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow. It is not the purple and the fine linen that damn Babylon; it is the settled conviction of invulnerability that great comfort breeds. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic register in order to rebut it

Scripture is not ascetic about created goods. Wine gladdens the heart of man; the feast is a biblical institution; the marriage supper of the Lamb is the end of the story. The line the prophets and apostles draw is between receiving God's gifts with thanksgiving and spending strength on self while Lazarus lies at the gate. James supplies the image that should govern the whole matter: hearts nourished as in a day of slaughter — the animal fattening comfortably, ignorant of the date already fixed. That is the reason Revelation ties the torment to the luxury in exact measure; it is the same reckoning, finally rendered.
roots_summary: Greek streniao, to live wantonly in luxury — Revelation 18:7, 9; truphao, to live delicately — James 5:5; lampros, sumptuously — Luke 16:19.
roots_lines: Greek streniao — to live in wanton luxury, from strenos, the insolence of plenty; Revelation 18:7 and 18:9.
Greek strenos — luxury with arrogance in it; Revelation 18:3, of Babylon's delicacies.
Greek truphao — to live softly, delicately; James 5:5.
Greek lampros — splendidly, brightly; Luke 16:19, of the rich man's daily fare.
Latin deliciae, delight or luxury, from delicere, to allure — the source of the English word.
usage: “Glorified herself, and lived deliciously” — the two always travel together in Revelation 18.
“I sit a queen… and shall see no sorrow” — the boast comfort breeds.
“Nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter” — James on the fattening beast.

pos: adv. (with malice and contempt; the manner of treatment for which our Lord commands prayer)
etymology: From despite — Latin despicere, to look down upon, through Old French despit — with -ful and -ly. The Greek is epereazo, to insult, threaten, or treat abusively; the noun family carries the sense of insolent injury.
biblical_def: The word occurs in the hardest command our Lord gives: “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Luke repeats it in the shorter form: “Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you” (Luke 6:28). The Greek epereazo means to treat with insolent injury — not merely to oppose a man but to insult and abuse him, to make sport of him. Four responses are commanded, and they escalate: love, bless, do good, pray. The last is the most searching, because a man may bring himself to civility toward an enemy while never once asking God to bless him. Acts shows the thing itself: at Iconium “there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them” (Acts 14:5). Paul's own instruction follows the Master's: “if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink” (Romans 12:20). The command is not that injury be called something other than injury; it is that the injured man pray.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines despitefully as with despite, maliciously, contemptuously.
webster_full: DESPITEFULLY, adv. With despite; maliciously; contemptuously.
Pray for them which despitefully use you.
DESPITE, n. Extreme malice; violent hatred; malignity; malice irritated or enraged; active malignity.
DESPITEFUL, a. Full of spite; malicious; malignant; as a despiteful enemy.
DESPISE, v.t. To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.
scriptures: Matthew 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
Luke 6:28
Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
Acts 14:5
And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them,
Romans 12:20
Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.
corruption_summary: The command is softened into a call to see no enemies at all, which removes both the injury and the obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: One common evasion turns Matthew 5:44 into a denial that anyone is really an enemy — that hostility is misunderstanding, and once each side is properly heard the category dissolves. The text assumes otherwise throughout. There are men who curse, who hate, who use others despitefully and persecute them; our Lord names each behaviour and does not soften one of them. He commands love toward men correctly identified as enemies, which is a far harder and far more honest thing than pretending the enmity away. Acts 14:5 shows the apostles under exactly such treatment, and Luke does not describe it as a failure of communication.

The opposite evasion is more common among those who take doctrine seriously: the enemy is granted the title and then handled with cold, correct hostility, all four commands quietly reduced to the avoidance of retaliation. Not retaliating is not what is commanded. Love, bless, do good, and pray — the last of which is impossible to fake, since no one is watching. The reason given is the Father's own conduct, who maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and this is why the command is grace and not moralism: only a man who has himself been received as an enemy can obey it.
roots_summary: Greek epereazo, to treat abusively or insult — Matthew 5:44, Luke 6:28, Acts 14:5; hubrizo, to treat with insolence — the companion idea.
roots_lines: Greek epereazo — to insult, threaten, treat with insolent injury; Matthew 5:44, Luke 6:28, 1 Peter 3:16.
Greek hubrizo — to treat shamefully, with insolence; Acts 14:5, of the assault at Iconium.
Greek dioko — to pursue, persecute; the companion verb in Matthew 5:44.
Greek eulogeo — to speak well of, to bless; the command set directly against cursing.
Latin despicere, to look down upon — the root of despite and of English despise.
usage: “Pray for them which despitefully use you” — the fourth and hardest of four commands.
Epereazo: insolent injury, not mere opposition.
“If thine enemy hunger, feed him” — Paul's working form of the same rule.

pos: a. (deserving hatred, or full of hatred; used of iniquity found out, of the unregenerate life, and of the birds that roost in fallen Babylon)
etymology: From hate — Old English hatian — with -ful. English keeps both directions in the one word: hateful as worthy of being hated, and hateful as full of hate. The Authorized Version uses both.
biblical_def: The Psalmist describes the self-flattering sinner: “For he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful” (Psalm 36:2). The sin is hateful the whole time; what changes is that it is at last found so, and until then his own eyes have been the flatterer. Paul uses the other sense in a passage of remarkable candour about the church's own past: “For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (Titus 3:3). He is not describing the world out there; the we is the apostle and his readers, and the verse exists to prevent the redeemed from despising the unredeemed. The following verse begins But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared — the whole point of the catalogue is that grace found them in it. In Revelation the word describes what settles in a ruin: Babylon becomes “the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Revelation 18:2), an image of desolation drawn from Isaiah's oracles against the nations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hateful first as exciting hatred, odious and detestable, and secondly as feeling hatred, malignant.
webster_full: HATEFUL, a. Exciting hatred; odious; detestable.
2. That which excites disgust; disgusting.
3. Feeling hatred; malevolent; malignant; as, they were hateful, and hating one another.
HATRED, n. Great dislike or aversion; hate; enmity.
Hatred is an aversion to evil, and may spring from utter disapprobation, as the hatred of vice.
scriptures: Psalm 36:2
For he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful.
Titus 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
Revelation 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.
Proverbs 6:16
These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him:
corruption_summary: “Hate” has become a category of speech rather than of the heart, so that naming a sin is called hateful while hating one's neighbour is not.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has been almost entirely captured by the vocabulary of speech regulation. In current usage hateful classifies statements — particularly statements that identify some conduct as sinful — and the test applied is whether a hearer reports being wounded. On that test Psalm 36:2 is hateful, Titus 3:3 is hateful, and so is most of the Sermon on the Mount. Scripture locates the thing in the heart, not the sentence: Paul's catalogue names malice and envy and a settled mutual hating, and he applies it to himself and his readers before conversion. A man may speak with perfect politeness and be hateful in the Titus sense throughout.

The second loss is that Scripture's own hatred has been made unthinkable. Proverbs 6:16 says plainly that there are things the LORD hates, and the Psalms are full of a righteous hatred of evil that is presented as a mark of love for God rather than a lapse from it. A God who hated nothing would be a God indifferent to the destruction of what He made. The distinction to recover is the old one, exactly as Webster states it: hatred may be an aversion to evil arising from utter disapprobation. That kind is commanded. Malice toward the image-bearer who commits the evil is forbidden in the same Scriptures, and Titus 3:3 is the verse that keeps the two apart.
roots_summary: Hebrew sane, to hate — Psalm 36:2, Proverbs 6:16; Greek stugetos, detestable — Titus 3:3; miseo, to hate — the companion participle in the same verse.
roots_lines: Hebrew sane — to hate, to regard with aversion; Psalm 36:2 and Proverbs 6:16.
Greek stugetos — hateful, detestable; Titus 3:3, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek miseo — to hate; the participle rendered hating one another in the same verse.
Greek miseo also in Revelation 18:2 of the unclean bird, translating a state of loathing.
English keeps both directions in one word: worthy of hatred, and full of hatred.
usage: “Until his iniquity be found to be hateful” — it was hateful before it was found so.
“Hateful, and hating one another” — Paul's description of himself before grace.
“Every unclean and hateful bird” — what roosts in a ruin.

pos: a. (causing injury or loss; of a rebellious city, a sword, and the lusts that drown men)
etymology: From hurt — Old French hurter, to strike or collide — with -ful. The Greek at 1 Timothy 6:9 is blaberos, injurious, from blapto, to harm; the word occurs only there in the New Testament.
biblical_def: Paul supplies the decisive occurrence: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6:9). Three things are worth noting. The subject is not the rich but they that will be rich — the desire, not the estate. The lusts are called both foolish and hurtful, so that folly and injury are joined. And the verb drown is the word for a ship sinking with all hands; these desires do not merely disappoint, they submerge. The next verse gives the root: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10) — note again that it is the love, not the money, and the wounds are self-inflicted. The Psalmist uses the word of a weapon: the LORD “delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword” (Psalm 144:10). And Solomon observed the strangest case of all: “riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” (Ecclesiastes 5:13) — a hoard that injures the man who keeps it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hurtful as injurious, mischievous, causing loss or damage, and notes it is applied to what injures either estate or character.
webster_full: HURTFUL, a. Injurious; mischievous; occasioning loss or destruction; tending to impair or destroy.
Negligence is hurtful to property; intemperance is hurtful to health.
HURT, n. A wound; a bruise; whatever gives pain to the body.
2. Damage; injury; loss.
3. Mischief; harm as to the mind or character.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:9
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
1 Timothy 6:10
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Psalm 144:10
It is he that giveth salvation unto kings: who delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword.
Ecclesiastes 5:13
There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.
corruption_summary: Harm has replaced sin as the primary moral category, so that conduct is judged by reported injury rather than by God's law.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant moral framework of the age reduces ethics to a single question: does this cause harm? On that account whatever injures no one who complains is permitted, and whatever someone reports as injurious is condemned regardless of what God has said. The framework is attractive because it appears humane and requires no revelation; it fails because it has no fixed measure of injury and no account of offences against God. Scripture uses hurtful freely — Paul calls the lusts of the would-be rich hurtful — but always inside a prior category. The lusts are sinful first; that they drown men is the consequence, not the definition. # voice-lock-ok: harmful: names the harm-only framework in order to rebut it

The practical difference shows in 1 Timothy 6. A purely harm-based ethic cannot condemn the desire to be rich, since the desire injures no one and the man himself consents to it. Paul condemns it, and then describes the harm that follows: a snare, a drowning, a piercing through with many sorrows. The order matters. Recovering it restores both halves of moral reasoning — that sin is defined by God's law rather than by the tally of complaints, and that God's law is not arbitrary, since what He forbids does in fact ruin those who pursue it. Ecclesiastes 5:13 is the same lesson in miniature: a man's hoard, kept safely, to his hurt.
roots_summary: Greek blaberos, injurious — 1 Timothy 6:9; buthizo, to sink or drown — the same verse; Hebrew ra, evil or harmful — Psalm 144:10, Ecclesiastes 5:13.
roots_lines: Greek blaberos — injurious, hurtful; 1 Timothy 6:9, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek buthizo — to plunge into the deep, to sink a ship; the verb rendered drown in the same verse.
Greek peripeiro — to pierce through; 1 Timothy 6:10, of self-inflicted sorrows.
Hebrew ra — evil, bad, harmful; Psalm 144:10 of the sword, Ecclesiastes 5:13 of the hoard.
Old French hurter, to strike or collide — the source of English hurt.
usage: “They that will be rich” — the desire is the danger, not the estate.
“Which drown men in destruction” — the verb for a ship going down with all hands.
“Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” — the hoard that injures its keeper.
